results.title: A First Comprehensive Study of TurboQuant: Accuracy and Performance | vLLM Blog
results.content:
Takeaway: TurboQuant consistently underperforms both BF16 and FP8 by reducing throughput and increasing per-token latency. However, in memory-constrained serving scenarios, the KV-cache compression prevents memory saturation and dramatically reduces TTFT under burst load relative to BF16. This is the core of TurboQuant's value proposition: it trades per-token speed for the ability to serve requests that would otherwise be queued. FP8, on the other hand, provides the best of both worlds: it [...] TurboQuant 4bit-nc offers a compelling memory-for-throughput tradeoff. This variant provides up to 3.4x KV-cache capacity with modest accuracy degradation of 1-4 points on most benchmarks. It is particularly valuable for memory-constrained deployments where the TTFT improvement at burst load outweighs the negative impact on all other metrics. Thoroughly validate accuracy on the target workload before deploying. [...] The throughput results reinforce the latency findings. FP8 matches BF16 throughput on both models. All TurboQuant variants are strictly below BF16: on Qwen3-30B (Figure 9), ranging from 80% (k8v4) to 73% (3bit-nc); on Llama-70B (Figure 10), from 75% (k8v4 and 4bit-nc) to 66% (3bit-nc). More aggressive quantization consistently yields lower throughput — the dequantization overhead grows with the complexity of the packing format.

results.title: Google’s TurboQuant: The Compression Breakthrough That Could Reshape LLM Infrastructure | by Akshay Kalane | Towards AI
results.content:
TurboQuant is not the only KV cache compression method arriving at ICLR 2026. NVIDIA’s KVTC (Key-Value Transform Coding) uses a PCA-based decorrelation approach inspired by JPEG compression and claims up to 20x compression with less than 1 percentage point accuracy penalty. [...] On March 24, 2026, Google Research published a paper called TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate, set to be presented at ICLR 2026 in Rio de Janeiro. Within 48 hours, memory chip stocks fell, developers had ported the algorithm to llama.cpp and Apple’s MLX framework, and Cloudflare’s CEO was calling it “Google’s DeepSeek moment.”

So what exactly is TurboQuant, how does it work under the hood, and why does it matter for anyone building AI systems today? [...] As of this writing, Google has not released official open-source code. Community implementations are independent reproductions based on the paper and pseudocode. Official code is widely expected around Q2 2026.

## The Competitive Landscape

>  ⚡ The headline numbers are striking but contested — 8x throughput and 6x memory reduction on H100s, but measured under specific conditions that may not generalize to typical production workloads. These are extraordinary claims by any standard in quantization research. The benchmark conditions that produced these numbers matter enormously, and we’ll examine them closely in the next section, the Google TurboQuant benchmark methodology is where the real scrutiny belongs. [...] selected because they put the technique in the best possible light. TurboQuant accuracy loss tradeoffs also interact with throughput measurements in ways that need to be disentangled before the 8x number can be taken at face value.

results.title: What Is Google TurboQuant and What Does It Mean for Open Source Inference? - Deep Infra
results.content: Reducing KV cache memory by 4 to 6x through TurboQuant-style compression has two direct effects on inference economics. First, it allows more concurrent requests on the same GPU, which improves throughput and reduces cost per completion. Second, it makes genuinely long context workloads more practical without requiring providers to throw additional hardware at the problem. [...] It is worth being clear about the current state. TurboQuant was presented at ICLR 2026 in April and Google’s official implementation has not yet been publicly released as of this writing, with a release expected around Q2 2026. [...] The closed source labs will use TurboQuant internally. But the open source community is already implementing it, and inference providers running open source models will be able to apply it across their entire model catalog rather than one proprietary system. That is the structural advantage of open inference infrastructure. Every efficiency breakthrough in the research community shows up across every model, not just the ones a single lab decides to optimize.
